title: Committing to a vertical: 10 Riftbeast

video.title: I Summoned the Entire Jungle... 10 Riftbeast Is Absolutely Busted!!

player.name: Robinsongz
player.about: High-level player and author of the TFT Handbook; explains positioning changes between rounds more than most streamers.

summary: Launch-week game in which Robin hits the prismatic 10-Riftbeast breakpoint and runs the lobby over with the summoned jungle. A vertical-trait game from the decision to commit to the capped board.
thesis: A vertical is the one line where the tier list matters less than the question 'can I actually reach the breakpoint?' The commitment is made from emblems and augments, not from wanting to. This game shows what it takes: an early decision, every copy bought, items on the units that stay, and positioning around a board that grows summons. Watch how early the commitment happens and what he would have needed to see to abandon it.

timeline.title: The augment that makes the vertical possible
timeline.watch: Which augment or emblem tips the decision toward a Riftbeast vertical, and what the board holds at that moment. A vertical at 10 needs an emblem source; find it.
timeline.why: Verticals that reach their top breakpoint are decided by an emblem or a trait augment, not by rolling harder. Without that source the correct play is the flexible board.
timeline.question: Without the emblem source, what is the highest Riftbeast breakpoint he could reach at level 8, and would it still be worth playing?

timeline.title: Buying every copy and fielding the count
timeline.watch: How the early Riftbeast units are bought and fielded even when a stronger non-Riftbeast unit is available. Count the trait number on the board each round.
timeline.why: A vertical's stage-2 strength comes from the breakpoint, and each breakpoint is a step; skipping one for a stronger single unit loses the streak the trait would have bought.

timeline.title: Items on the units that stay
timeline.watch: Which Riftbeast units receive the items and whether any item goes on a unit that is later replaced when the board grows.
timeline.why: In a vertical the final roster is known early, so items can go straight to their final holders; that is the one luxury the line offers.

timeline.title: Levels for slots, not for odds
timeline.watch: Level timings in a vertical: each level is one more trait body. Watch whether he levels on schedule or earlier because the breakpoint needs the slot.
timeline.why: For a vertical the value of a level is a slot toward the breakpoint; that can justify leveling a round early even at the cost of interest.

timeline.title: The prismatic breakpoint arrives
timeline.watch: The round the tenth Riftbeast is fielded and what changed on the board to make room: which non-Riftbeast unit left, and whether an emblem was moved.
timeline.why: Top breakpoints are usually one emblem and one level away for most of the game; the moment they land, the board changes shape and so should the positioning.
timeline.question: Which unit did the tenth slot cost him, and was that unit doing more than the breakpoint adds?

timeline.title: Positioning a board that summons
timeline.watch: Where the summoned units spawn relative to his frontline and how he positions the carries so the summons take the hits. Note the changes between opponents.
timeline.why: Summons are extra bodies; a board with extra bodies wants its carries farther back and its tanks where the summons appear, not the default layout.

timeline.title: Capping a vertical
timeline.watch: Once the breakpoint is fielded: does the gold go to two-starring the carries, to a ninth unit, or to more rolls? Which is worth more for a capped vertical.
timeline.why: A vertical at its top breakpoint caps by upgrading the units inside it; a ninth slot outside the trait adds less than a 2-star inside it.

questions.q: What has to be true before committing to a 10-trait vertical?
questions.a: An emblem source (augment or emblem) that makes the top breakpoint reachable at a level you can hit, and a stage-2 board that can field the trait count without bleeding out. Wanting it is not enough.

questions.q: Why can a vertical level earlier than the standard timing?
questions.a: Because each level is one more trait body and the breakpoints pay per body; the extra slot can be worth more than the interest lost, which is never true for a flexible board.

questions.q: What is the failure mode of this line?
questions.a: Committing without the emblem source and getting stuck one unit short of the breakpoint for three stages, bleeding HP with a board that is neither vertical nor strong.

sourceNote: Title, channel, date, length and the fact that the game reaches the prismatic 10-Riftbeast breakpoint come from the video page. The stage guide is TFT Lab's reading of a vertical game; the video has no creator chapters, so stops are anchored to stages.
